opus-5.5.text:
I think what strikes me most is that the reasoning ability seems to transfer in ways we didn't explicitly train for. When you look at how these o1-style models are trained, most of the reinforcement learning signal comes from domains where answers can be verified, like math competition problems and coding tasks with unit tests. Those are fairly narrow. But once the model learns to think in long chains, to backtrack, to say "wait, this doesn't look right, let me check again," that behavior shows up in other areas too. It shows up in logic puzzles, in scientific questions, and even in some writing and planning tasks where there's no verifier at all.

To me that suggests the model isn't just memorizing solution templates for math. It's picking up something more like a meta-skill, a habit of self-reflection and search. In earlier pretraining-centric paradigms, we mostly got better by adding more data from the target distribution. Here you train on a relatively small set of hard, checkable problems, and the gain spreads outward. That's quite different, and honestly a bit surprising.

At the same time, I want to be careful. The generalization isn't uniform. On tasks that need real-world knowledge or that are very open-ended, longer thinking doesn't always help, and sometimes the model overthinks and talks itself into a worse answer. So the interesting research question for me is: what exactly is being transferred? Is it the reasoning patterns themselves, or is RL mainly unlocking abilities that were already latent from pretraining? My current intuition is that it's largely the latter. Pretraining builds the knowledge and the raw capacity, and RL on verifiable tasks teaches the model how to use that capacity more deliberately. If that's right, it has big implications for how we should allocate compute between pretraining and post-training going forward.

fable-5.1.text:
What strikes me most is that the generalization in O-like models doesn't look the way we were trained to expect it to look.

For years, the mental model in machine learning was: you train on a distribution, you test on something close to that distribution, and anything beyond that is out of scope. Generalization meant interpolation within a fairly narrow neighborhood. What we see with these reasoning models is different in kind. You train on math and code, where you have verifiable rewards, and then the model gets better at things nobody wrote a reward for. It gets better at reading a legal contract carefully. It gets better at catching its own mistakes in a translation. It gets more cautious about claims it can't support.

I think the reason is that what's being learned isn't the answer to math problems. It's a set of behaviors around thinking. Things like: check your work before committing. When you hit a dead end, back up instead of pushing forward. Break a hard question into smaller ones. Try an alternative when the first approach stalls. Those are not domain-specific skills. Math and code just happen to be the places where you can measure, cheaply and precisely, whether the behavior paid off. So they become the training ground, but the thing you're actually shaping is more like a cognitive habit.

There's a second point that I find just as interesting. Pre-training already contains most of these patterns. Humans write out their reasoning constantly, in textbooks, in forum threads, in proofs. The base model has seen all of it. Reinforcement learning isn't teaching the model to reason from scratch. It's selecting and reinforcing patterns that were already latent, and making the model willing to spend more tokens on them. That's a very different picture from "RL discovers new capabilities." It's closer to "RL changes what the model chooses to do with what it already knows."

That also explains why the transfer is uneven. It generalizes well to anything that benefits from careful step-by-step verification. It generalizes much less well to things that need taste, or world knowledge the model simply doesn't have. Reasoning longer doesn't help if the missing ingredient is a fact.

So the compelling part, to me, is that we've found a way to improve a very general behavior through a very narrow training signal. The open question is how far that goes. Whether it eventually hits a ceiling defined by what's recoverable from pre-training, or whether, with enough environments and enough scale, the model starts building genuinely new strategies. I honestly don't know the answer yet, and that's exactly why it's the thing I pay the most attention to.

astra-6.text:
What I find most compelling is the possibility that these models are learning something more general than how to answer a particular kind of question. They may be learning useful problem-solving behaviors—breaking a problem down, checking an assumption, or revising an approach when it doesn’t work. If those behaviors transfer to unfamiliar tasks, that’s a powerful form of generalization.

But I’d distinguish doing better on new examples from doing better on genuinely new kinds of problems. A model can look very strong when the underlying structure is familiar. The more interesting test is what happens when that structure changes: can it recognize what matters, choose a useful strategy, and catch its own mistakes?

So, for me, the exciting question is whether giving a model more time to reason helps it handle situations that its training didn’t directly prepare it for. That would make reasoning a much broader capability.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find most compelling is the possibility that a model can learn a way of solving problems that transfers beyond the problems it was trained on. It might learn to break a task into parts, check an intermediate result, or reconsider an approach when it reaches a contradiction. Those habits could be useful across many domains.

But I think we have to be careful about what we call generalization. Doing well on another math benchmark is different from handling a problem with unfamiliar assumptions, incomplete information, or no easy way to verify the answer. The interesting question is whether the model knows when its approach applies—and when it needs to change that approach.

So for me, the exciting possibility is that additional reasoning time becomes a broadly useful resource. Can the model use that time to identify uncertainty and correct mistakes, rather than simply produce a longer explanation? That would be a meaningful step forward.
